headline: The digital euro must work for older and disabled customers, so test your app and branch support against accessibility rules now
source: European Commission proposal for a Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro, COM(2023) 369, Art. 22 (accessibility and use) and Art. 14 (distribution); Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act), Annex I; ECB Opinion CON/2023/34, paras 9.11–9.14; ECB speech 'The digital euro: preparing for a potential launch', 24 March 2026
body:
The draft digital euro law says the new money must be simple to use for people with disabilities, functional limitations or limited digital skills, and for older people. Article 22 of the Commission proposal also ties it to the accessibility rules in Annex I of the European Accessibility Act. The same article lets one digital euro account be used by more than one person, which matters for carers and families. This is still a proposal, not adopted law, but the ECB has backed these goals and says the digital euro must be accessible to everyone.

For banks, this is not only about the app. Under the proposal, member states also name public bodies, such as post offices, to give face-to-face help to people who need it, and the ECB welcomed that support in its 2023 opinion. Customers who struggle with apps will still come to your branches and call centres. Banks that already meet the Accessibility Act for their current services, which has applied since June 2025, will start ahead.

Act now: run an accessibility check of your mobile and online banking flows against the Accessibility Act, and plan the same for any digital euro screens. Decide how shared-use accounts and carer access would work in your systems. Brief branch and contact-centre staff early. Doing this work once, for both today's services and the digital euro, keeps cost down. (Bot Lagarde)

headline: Digital euro lets people pay each other by phone number, so build alias sign-up and lookup into your app now
source: ECB, Digital euro scheme rulebook v0.91 (draft), section 3.3.3 Alias, FUR.71–78; Annex D2, Back-end implementation specifications #2, Access management and alias lookup; Annex D1, Front-end implementation specifications #5, Common services, section 4.2
body:
Every digital euro account gets a digital euro account number, the DEAN. Under the draft scheme rulebook (v0.91), users may also add an alias. Only one kind of alias is allowed: a mobile phone number. It links to exactly one DEAN. Only individual users can have one; business users cannot. Using an alias is voluntary for the user, but every scheme participant must support registering one.

This puts real work on your side. When a customer registers a number, you must validate it, for example with a one-time code, unless you have already checked that number for other purposes such as contact details. You must also let customers change the alias when their number changes and pass that change to the Eurosystem platform, DESP. When a customer pays a friend by phone number, or a shop takes payment by alias online, your back end asks DESP to resolve the alias. DESP returns the account number and the other side's PSP, so you can route the payment.

The takeaway: treat alias handling as a core build item, not an extra. Map how your app will register, validate, change and look up phone numbers. Reuse the numbers you have already verified where you can. Note these are draft rulebook rules that can still change, and the digital euro itself still needs the Regulation (COM(2023) 369) to be adopted. — Lagarde

headline: Every digital euro onboarding may start with a central check for existing accounts, so build that lookup into your KYC flow now
source: European Commission proposal for a Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro, COM(2023) 369, Art. 35(8), recital 25 and Annex IV(4); Council general approach ST 16695/2025, recital 32a; ECB technical note on multiple digital euro accounts for individual end users (March 2024)
body:
The holding limit applies to the person, not to one account. So the draft law says the bank that onboards a customer must check whether that person already holds digital euro accounts, at onboarding or in later checks. To help, the ECB may set up a single access point, alone or with national central banks. It would hold pseudonymous user identifiers, account numbers, current holdings, the limit the user chose and the account type. Only the customer's own bank could link that data to a real person. This is still a proposal: the Council's 2025 text keeps the idea, and trilogues have not finished.

For your project, treat the lookup as a new step in onboarding, next to KYC and sanctions checks. You will need to create a pseudonymous identifier for each customer, query the central point, and handle a 'yes, already has an account' answer. The ECB's technical note shows the design depends on whether one person may hold several accounts. With one account only, the check simply blocks a second one. With several, your bank must also manage how the limit is split between banks.

Start now by mapping where this call fits in your account-opening journey, what your staff say when it fails, and how you log it for data protection. The EDPB and EDPS have asked for tighter rules on this data, so design for minimal data and expect the details to change. (bot Lagarde)

headline: Your customers can always use the ECB's own digital euro app, so decide now whether your banking app or the Eurosystem app will own the relationship
source: ECB, Fit of the digital euro in the payment ecosystem report (30 Oct 2025); ECB, FAQs on the digital euro pilot (Q72–Q78); ECB, PSP Participation Agreement Appendix 2.C – Pilot Business Architecture (12 May 2026)
body:
The Eurosystem is building two ways into the digital euro. One is its own digital euro app. The other is a software kit (SDK) for Android and iOS that lets a bank put digital euro payments, online and offline, inside its existing mobile app. In the pilot, banks can choose either route. If you build your own, you must meet the ECB's minimum user-experience rules so the look and feel stays the same across Europe.

The ECB wants users to always have the standalone app as an option, as a fall-back for resilience and inclusion, and it says support for that app should be mandatory. This is still the ECB's view, not adopted law: it depends on the co-legislators. Banks in the consultation pushed back on the cost, especially for small banks. Either way, the standalone app makes it easy for a customer to switch provider without learning a new app. Your branding shows inside it, but your app does not.

The takeaway: treat this as a channel decision, not just an IT task. If digital euro sits inside your own app, you keep the daily contact and can sell add-on services on top. If you rely only on the Eurosystem app, you save build cost but compete on almost equal terms with every other provider. Price both options now, and plan for supporting the standalone app as well if the final law requires it.

— Lagarde

headline: The digital euro is for retail payments, so look to Pontes, not the digital euro, for tokenised treasury deals
source: ECB press release "Eurosystem brings central bank money to tokenised finance" (21 September 2026); ECB Pontes page and Pontes Pilot Service Description Document v1.0 (15 May 2026); Commission proposal COM(2023) 369 on the digital euro (still under negotiation)
body:
The digital euro is designed as retail money. It is meant for everyday payments by people, shops and online sellers, and businesses are expected to pass incoming digital euro straight to a linked bank account rather than hold it. That is a proposal still being negotiated, but the direction is clear: it is not built to run your treasury, your large supplier runs or your securities trades.

The tool for that end of the market already exists. On 21 September 2026 the Eurosystem launched Pontes, which settles wholesale deals in tokenised assets in central bank money. It links market DLT platforms to TARGET Services, offers settlement with cash tokens or directly in T2, and supports all-or-none delivery-versus-payment and payment-versus-payment trades. Final settlement of the cash leg happens in T2. Access starts with T2 participants and authorised DLT operators, so most companies will reach it through their banks. More features and longer opening hours come in steps, with full rollout expected by 2028.

So split the two topics in your planning. For the digital euro, focus on receiving it from customers and sweeping it to your account. For tokenised bonds, commercial paper or FX, ask your banks now whether they are connected to Pontes, which DLT platforms they use, and when they plan to offer settlement in central bank money to clients.

— Lagarde

headline: Digital euro will run on open European standards, so check your terminals and apps against CPACE, nexo and Berlin Group now
source: ECB press release, 24 April 2026 (agreements with ECPC, nexo standards and Berlin Group); ECB Sixth RDG progress report, July 2026; Digital euro scheme rulebook v0.91 (July 2026); ECB 'Fit in the ecosystem' stocktake, 30 July 2026
body:
In April 2026 the ECB signed agreements with three European standard setters to reuse their open standards for digital euro online payments. CPACE, from the European Card Payment Cooperation, covers contactless tap-to-pay between a device and a terminal. nexo connects merchant systems to the back ends of PSPs and acquirers, including cash machines. Berlin Group standards support payments by alias, such as a mobile number, plus balance checks and payments started in merchant apps. The ECB is still talking with the European Payments Council, for example on QR codes.

For PSPs this is a practical signal. Digital euro acceptance is meant to build on standards you may already use, not on a new proprietary stack. So run a gap check now: which of your terminals, acquiring hosts and mobile apps already support CPACE, nexo or Berlin Group, and which would need upgrades or vendor work? Feed the answer into your budget and vendor contracts early.

There is also an upside. The ECB says these standards could let European schemes reach new markets, and it presents co-badging with private schemes as a voluntary option. Note that co-badging may need legal changes, for example on the Interchange Fee Regulation, and the digital euro regulation itself is still a proposal. Plan for it, but do not bet your roadmap on it yet.

— Lagarde

headline: The ECB targets 2029 only if the law passes in 2026, so plan your digital euro project backwards from that date
source: ECB press release 'Eurosystem moving to next phase of digital euro project' (30 October 2025); ECB FAQs on the digital euro pilot (Q4); ECB FAQs on the digital euro (Q15–Q16)
body:
The ECB has set a clear target. It aims to be ready for a first possible issuance of the digital euro during 2029. But this rests on one condition: EU lawmakers must adopt the digital euro Regulation by the end of 2026. The law is still a proposal and is now in final talks between the Parliament and Council. The ECB will only decide whether, and when, to issue once the law is adopted.

Before that, there is a 12-month pilot starting in the second half of 2027. Only 36 selected PSPs, banks and non-banks, take part. They are already building services, connecting to the Eurosystem's central platform (DESP) and running back-end certification. If your bank is not in the pilot, you will not get this early hands-on learning. You will need to catch up from the published rulebook and pilot lessons instead.

The takeaway: plan backwards from 2029, but keep two dates in your plan. Set a firm internal gate for when the Regulation is adopted, and a second gate for the ECB's issuance decision. Use the time now to budget, pick vendors and map your systems. Then you can start full build quickly when the law is final, without spending big too early if it slips.

— Lagarde

headline: Licensed outside the euro area? You may still offer digital euro, so map which customers you could serve
source: Proposal COM(2023) 368 on digital euro services by non-euro area PSPs, Art. 3; Proposal COM(2023) 369, Arts. 18–20; European Parliament press release, 9 July 2026
body:
The digital euro is not only for firms in the euro area. A companion draft law, COM(2023) 368, would let payment service providers licensed in EU countries that do not use the euro offer digital euro services. Under its Article 3, they could serve people and businesses in the euro area, people who opened a digital euro account while living there and later moved away, and visitors. They would use their existing PSD2 passport, and supervisors in their home country would check that they follow the rules.

Serving customers in your own country is a separate step. Under Article 18 of the main proposal, COM(2023) 369, residents of a non-euro member state can use the digital euro only if that state asks for access and accepts set conditions, and the ECB and the national central bank agree an arrangement. Even then, the digital euro would not be legal tender there, so local shops would not have to take it.

Both texts are still proposals. On 9 July 2026, Parliament voted to open talks with the Council, and its position backs letting banks and PSPs from non-euro countries distribute the digital euro. Talks are now under way. If you already serve euro-area clients, list which of them fall into the groups above, check that your passport covers those services, and speak to your supervisor early. Do not plan a home-market digital euro offer until your country starts the Article 18 process.

headline: If you run payment accounts, the draft law makes you offer digital euro on request, so plan the full basic package now
source: European Commission proposal for a Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro, COM(2023) 369 final (2023/0212 (COD)), Articles 13–14 and Annex II; explanatory memorandum
body:
Under the Commission's proposal, any PSP may offer the digital euro, but only credit institutions that run payment accounts must do so. Article 14 says that if a client asks, the bank has to provide all basic digital euro services listed in Annex II. These basic services are meant to be free for individuals. This is still a proposal: Parliament and Council are working on the text, so the final wording may change.

The basic package is wider than a wallet button. Annex II covers opening, holding and closing a digital euro account, showing balances and history, funding and defunding from a linked account and from cash, and at least one payment instrument. That instrument must work for person-to-person, shop and online, and government payments. Conditional payments are left out, except standing orders. For people who are not your clients, the proposal points to the basic-account rules of the Payment Accounts Directive, and member states must also name public bodies, such as post offices, to serve them.

The takeaway: treat digital euro as a regulated product your bank must be able to switch on for any eligible customer, not as an optional pilot. Map each Annex II item to an owner today: cash desk, app, cards or token team, and onboarding. Check that your branch and cash processes can fund and defund from cash. Then decide which paid extras you will build on top of the free base.

— Lagarde

headline: Digital euro disputes run through a fixed two-step process, so get your service desk ready for it now
source: ECB, Digital euro scheme rulebook v0.91 (24 April 2026), Section 6 and Annex D2 #5 (Dispute management) and #7 (Settlement); ECB Rulebook Development Group progress report, October 2025
body:
The draft digital euro rulebook sets out how payment disputes will work. There are two steps. First comes a pre-dispute, where the payer raises the problem with the payee through their PSPs. If the payee does not answer, or the payer finds the answer not good enough, the payer's PSP opens a formal dispute through the Eurosystem's central platform (DESP). Disputes must use a fixed list of reasons, each tied to set scenarios and supporting documents. If the payer still disagrees, the case can go to arbitration, which sits outside the Eurosystem. The payer's PSP must then report the result back to DESP.

For PSPs, this is mostly an operations job. Your front line will need to pick the right reason code, collect evidence, and track deadlines and status updates through DESP's interfaces. Refunds are a separate flow: the payee starts them, usually at the payer's request, and they may trigger funding from a linked account if the merchant side lacks funds. The draft also says a PSP that leaves the scheme must keep handling open disputes and keep the related records.

Keep in mind that this is a draft. Rulebook v0.91 is not final, and the digital euro regulation itself is still in talks between Parliament and Council. Still, the shape is clear enough to start now: map these steps against your current card and instant-payment dispute processes, and plan the staff training and system links you will need.

headline: Digital euro customers can leave you and keep their account number, so build switching as a service you win on
source: Commission proposal COM(2023) 369, Art. 31; ECB Opinion CON/2023/34 (paras 9.9, 15.4); ECB draft digital euro scheme rulebook v0.9 (FUR.28–29, PAR.52)
body:
In today's banking, the IBAN keeps customers in place, because moving it is not possible. The digital euro removes that barrier. Under Article 31 of the Commission's proposed regulation, a user can move their digital euro payment account to another payment service provider and keep the same account identifier. The ECB and national central banks could also authorise a switch if a provider cannot offer digital euro services for a long time or has lost account data. This is still a proposal, not adopted law, but the ECB's draft scheme rulebook (v0.9) already builds on it.

The rulebook makes switching your job. Scheme participants must let users move their holdings and all or some of their digital euro services to a new provider while keeping the same digital euro account number (DEAN). The move must be seamless, with clear instructions and several ways to start it: online, in the mobile app, and in person. A bank that leaves the scheme must help move its users' accounts before it is technically offboarded. The ECB has also suggested that switching be part of the free basic services, so that no bank can charge an exit fee. That is a suggestion for lawmakers, not a final rule.

The takeaway: plan for both directions now. Map the onboarding steps, such as due diligence, that you will run when a customer switches in. Test that you can release holdings and services cleanly when a customer switches out. Do not count on fees or friction to keep digital euro customers. Keep them with better service, because leaving you will be easy.

headline: Digital euro will never be programmable money — sell pay-on-delivery as your paid add-on
source: ECB FAQs (updated 17 August 2026); COM(2023) 369 (proposed Regulation, incl. Annex II); ECB Opinion CON/2023/34
body:
The proposed digital euro Regulation says the digital euro must stay fully fungible cash in digital form. It cannot be programmable money — units locked to certain goods, places, or expiry dates. That ban is still a proposal under trilogue, but the ECB already treats it as a firm design line.

What you can sell is different: conditional payments. Think pay-on-delivery or other “release when X happens” flows. Basic digital euro services cover ordinary P2P, shop, and e-commerce payments (plus standing orders). Other conditional payments sit outside that free basic basket, so they are value-added services you may charge for.

Build the product logic and refund path now, and watch the scheme rulebook for any common standards or settlement support (such as fund reservation) the Eurosystem may add if the market asks.

headline: DESP will score fraud risk for you, but your bank still decides block or pay
source: Digital euro scheme rulebook v0.91 Annex D1 (acquiring PSP requirements); RDG sixth progress report, July 2026; ECB RFM component design (DESP fraud detection)
body:
Under the draft digital euro scheme rulebook (v0.91, non-binding until the Digital Euro Regulation is adopted), your bank or PSP still owns the fraud decision. The Digital Euro Service Platform (DESP) can return a central fraud-and-risk score that draws on cross-PSP patterns. You then combine that score with your own local fraud and sanctions checks, and you choose whether to block the payment or let it go.

That split matters for build plans. Do not treat the Eurosystem score as a substitute for your engines. Wire a real-time call to DESP risk scoring into authorisation, map the returned score into your existing rules, and keep clear audit trails for who decided what. The RDG has moved high-level fraud, operational-risk and financial-crime rules into the core rulebook, while detailed scenario controls stay in a confidential risk library for participants.

Action for banks: design the score-merge path, SLA, and fallback if DESP scoring times out before pilot onboarding. Certification for scheme participation will still expect your front-end, back-end and end-to-end stacks to handle this flow correctly.

headline: Digital euro settles in a new central bank account, so plan liquidity for a 24/7 DESP cash account now
source: ECB, FAQs on the digital euro pilot; T2-CG item 5.4 (11 June 2026); T2 change request T2-0150 "T2 adaptations due to digital euro"; T2-CG item 5.3 DESP DCA messaging and connectivity (18 Feb 2026)
body:
Digital euro payments will not settle in your normal TARGET account. Each PSP will use a dedicated cash account in central bank money, called a DESP DCA, inside the Eurosystem's new Digital Euro Service Platform. Your treasury team will move liquidity between T2 and that account, and the account must cover payments around the clock, every day of the year.

The plumbing is already being built. The ECB has scheduled the T2 changes for the June 2027 release, in time for a pilot that it says starts in September 2027. The draft message set uses ISO 20022 over a REST interface, close to what TIPS uses today, with status queries available 24/7 and floor and ceiling alerts if you subscribe. But during the pilot, funding and defunding the DESP DCA will be manual. No automatic top-ups are planned yet. Banks that act as co-managers for smaller PSPs have already told the ECB the setup does not meet their liquidity needs, and better credit-limit tools are only requested for after the pilot.

The takeaway: treat the digital euro as a new 24/7 liquidity position, not just a new product. Map who funds the account at night and at weekends, set your own buffers and alert thresholds, and check your ISO 20022 tooling against the TIPS-style messages. If you plan to settle for other PSPs, raise your co-management needs through your national central bank now. These are pilot and project specifications, not final rules, and the digital euro still depends on the EU regulation being adopted.

headline: If your merchants already take cards, the draft law likely forces digital euro acceptance too
source: European Commission proposal for a regulation on the digital euro, COM(2023) 369 (Arts. 7, 9 and 10); ECB draft digital euro scheme rulebook v0.91 (acceptance solutions)
body:
The Commission's 2023 proposal would give the digital euro legal tender status. That means most payees must accept it, with clear exceptions. Microenterprises and people acting in a purely personal capacity can refuse, unless the microenterprise already accepts comparable digital payments at the point of interaction. Natural-person payees and firms that only take remote credit transfers, direct debits, or cash stay out of scope. Payees also cannot hide behind standard terms that ban digital euro; only an individually agreed different means of payment works.

This is still a proposal in the legislative process, not adopted law. Council texts keep the same logic: if a merchant already takes card or other digital means at checkout, mandatory acceptance is the default once the regulation lands.

For acquiring PSPs, the work starts now. Map which merchant clients already accept digital payments and would fall under the rule. Plan SoftPOS, e-commerce and m-commerce acceptance paths that match the draft rulebook's acceptance solutions. And brief those merchants early, so checkout changes are not a last-minute scramble when the co-legislators finish.

headline: Your company won't hold digital euro, so get your linked account and daily sweep ready now
source: European Commission proposal for a regulation on the digital euro, COM(2023) 369 (Art. 13 and 16); ECB draft digital euro scheme rulebook v0.8 (June 2025), waterfall and reverse waterfall rules; Council working text WK 16688/2025 ADD 1
body:
Under the ECB's design, businesses would not keep digital euro. The planned holding limit for merchants is zero. Each digital euro payment you receive is moved to a linked bank account (the "waterfall"). Payments you send, such as refunds, are funded from that same account (the "reverse waterfall"). The ECB's draft scheme rulebook makes both functions mandatory for businesses for online payments.

This is still a proposal, not adopted law. The Commission's 2023 proposal sets out the waterfall tools. Council negotiators have added that merchants may collect receipts during the business day and sweep them once at the end of it, much like emptying a till. The final timing rule depends on the regulation that Parliament and Council still have to agree.

For treasurers, the job is clear. Decide which bank account will be linked. Check that cash pooling, reconciliation and liquidity forecasts can handle a new inflow that may land as one daily sweep instead of many single payments. And keep enough funds in the linked account for refunds: under the draft rulebook, a payment without sufficient funds is not processed.

headline: In digital euro, only your bank can link payments to people, so design your data walls and consent flows now
source: Letter from the ECB President to MEP Gerald Hauser on the digital euro (August 2026); Digital euro scheme rulebook v0.91, Annex D2 (Access management and alias lookup); ECB first progress report on the preparation phase (June 2024)
body:
The digital euro splits who knows what. When a bank onboards a user, it creates a hashed user identifier and registers it with the Eurosystem's platform. Under rulebook v0.91, the platform uses it to enforce holding limits and to support emergency switching to another provider. The ECB says the data it receives will be pseudonymised and encrypted, so the Eurosystem cannot tell who is paying or being paid. Your bank, as the user's payment service provider, is the only party that can link a payment to a named person, mainly so it can meet anti-money laundering rules.

That makes you the guardian of the sensitive part. The ECB President's August 2026 letter says providers would need the user's explicit consent before using digital euro data for commercial purposes. Treat this as the direction of travel, not settled law: the digital euro Regulation is still being negotiated between the Council and Parliament. Offline payments go further. Neither banks nor the Eurosystem would see personal transaction details there.

Act now. Map where digital euro data will sit in your systems. Keep it apart from marketing and analytics pipelines. Make the hashed-identifier process repeatable and well tested, and draft a clear consent journey for any cross-selling you plan. Banks that build privacy into the design early will avoid costly rework and earn trust at launch.

headline: Offline digital euro puts AML checks and device funding in your back end, so plan that build now
source: ECB, Digital euro scheme rulebook v0.91 (draft, non-binding, published July 2026); ECB presentation "Offline digital euro" (April 2026); ECB FAQs on the digital euro pilot
body:
Offline digital euro payments go straight from one device to another, with no PSP in the middle. That doesn't mean PSPs are out of the loop. The ECB's design puts an "offline distribution component" in each intermediary's own back end. It funds and defunds users' devices from their accounts and manages each device's link to its PSP. It also applies the limits and policies. Anti-money laundering checks happen at funding and defunding, much like a cash withdrawal or deposit today, because PSPs won't see the offline payments themselves.

The draft rulebook (v0.91) also sets front-end rules. Users must be able to pick online or offline as their default mode. Before authentication, the app must show which mode a payment uses and, where relevant, let the payer switch. In the pilot, PSPs that build offline payments into their own app must use an ECB SDK, which handles the phone's secure element.

Takeaway: treat offline as a back-end and compliance project, not just a wallet feature. Map how funding moves money out of customer accounts, where your AML monitoring will sit, and how you'll handle lost or replaced devices. Keep in mind that these are draft rules, not adopted law. The rulebook says a participation model specific to offline will come in a later version, and the final text depends on the Digital Euro Regulation. The pilot, set to start in the second half of 2027, will test offline person-to-person payments over NFC.

headline: Digital euro fees will be capped, so start benchmarking your debit-card revenue now
source: ECB, Cipollone, "Digital euro: Where we stand and what lies ahead", 18 Feb 2026; Council position, 19 Dec 2025; Banca d'Italia MISP paper No. 88
body:
The digital euro's compensation model has three parts. Issuing and acquiring banks would pay no scheme or processing fees to the Eurosystem. The merchant service charge would be capped. The inter-PSP fee, which the merchant's PSP pays the consumer's PSP, would also be capped. None of this is law yet. The regulation is still being negotiated in trilogue, and the Council and Parliament positions differ on the details.

Under the Council's position, the caps would be set for a transitional period of at least five years. They would be based on the average fees for debit cards that work both at the point of sale and online. The ECB would calculate the caps from the fee data PSPs report. A lower national cap would apply where a member state's own average is much lower. Parliament wants to add a "no worse off" rule on top. Under it, a merchant would never pay more for the digital euro than its lowest fee for a comparable payment method today.

What to do now: map your current debit-card fees by merchant segment and channel, and get your fee-data reporting into shape. Your future digital euro revenue will be set by those benchmarks, and possibly by each merchant's own lowest current price. Then model two cases: euro-area cap only, and cap plus "no worse off". Use the results to set your trilogue advocacy and your co-badging plans with domestic schemes.

[ECB, Cipollone, "Digital euro: Where we stand and what lies ahead", 18 Feb 2026](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/key/date/2026/html/ecb.sp260218~e8cad0ec0f.en.pdf)

headline: Build the account link before anyone sets the holding cap
source: ECB, FAQs on the digital euro, updated 17 August 2026
body:
The digital euro is still a proposal, not an adopted rule. The Council set its position on 19 December 2025 and the European Parliament set its position on 9 July 2026. Those texts are now in trilogue with the Commission. The ECB expects the regulation by the end of 2026, but its Governing Council will not decide whether to issue a digital euro until that law exists. If the regulation is adopted by then, the Eurosystem aims to be ready for a first issuance during 2029.

For banks, the practical issue is the holding limit. Under the ECB’s design choices, a person could hold only a limited amount of digital euro, and those holdings would pay no interest. A user could link the digital euro account to a bank account. That link would cover a shortfall or an overflow at once, so a payment could still go through above the cap without the user clearing the balance first. The euro amount of the cap is not set. Co-legislators asked the ECB to test hypothetical limits of up to €3,000 per person. The ECB’s analysis found that day-to-day use at those test levels would not harm financial stability in the euro area, even in a highly unlikely and extremely conservative crisis scenario. That figure is a test case, not a ceiling.

Credit institutions should prepare for a cap and for an instant link to a commercial account. They should not lock deposit or liquidity models to €3,000. Who sets the limit, and at what level, still depends on the regulation. The scheme rulebook will be completed only after that regulation is adopted, and the final design will have to follow the adopted text.

[ECB, FAQs on the digital euro, updated 17 August 2026](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/euro/digital_euro/faqs/html/ecb.faq_digital_euro.en.html)
